name: hungry grass

attributes.attribute: soil infected with the famine's memory that strikes a walker with insatiable hunger
grows over unmarked graves and where people died of hunger
the Great Hunger, the Irish famine of 1848 to 1850
a South American crop that thrived in Ireland and fed tenant families

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The hungry grass is an Irish folkloric site. It grew from the Irish Famine, called An Gorta Mór, the Great Hunger. English occupation denied Irish farmers the right to own land, so most lived as poor tenants of absent landlords. The potato, an import from South America, made this possible. It thrived in the rainy Irish climate. A small patch, even less than an acre, could feed a family. But a single crop invites famine when disease strikes. In 1848 to 1850 an airborne fungus turned stored potatoes into black slime. Cattle stood ready for market, yet most belonged to the landlords. Millions of tenant farmers starved. Ireland still exported food through the famine years, which bred bitterness and political strife. The population today is half of what it was before. Between one and one-and-a-half million people died; about the same number emigrated. From this tragedy came the legend. Patches of soil, infected with the memory of the famine, strike anyone who steps on them with insatiable hunger, so the person soon dies even though well fed. The hungry grass grows over unmarked graves, or wherever people died of hunger, by the roadside or in hovels.
objective: Document the hungry grass as a folkloric site born of the Irish Famine.
key_results: Record the fashions that caused the famine and its death and emigration toll.
Describe the hungry grass and the hunger it inflicts on those who step on it.
